title: Reading the Stories
summary: How biblical narrative works: the narrator's restraint, dialogue, repetition, key words, type-scenes, and structure; why the heroes are rarely models; and how story and history relate in the Bible's historical books.

sections.h: The Bible's most common kind of writing
sections.body:
More of the Bible is story than anything else. Genesis, much of Exodus and Numbers, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, the first half of Daniel, and Jonah in the Old Testament; the four Gospels and Acts in the New. Even books that are mostly law or prophecy are set inside a story: the laws of Exodus are given at a mountain on the way out of Egypt, and the prophecies of Jeremiah are interrupted by accounts of his arrest, his imprisonment in a cistern, and his forced exile to Egypt. The Bible does not begin with a creed or a list of rules. It begins with ‘In the beginning’, and much of what it teaches, it teaches by telling what happened.

This matters because narrative teaches differently from a law or a letter. A command says what to do. A letter argues. A story shows, and leaves the reader to see. Most misreadings of biblical narrative come from reading a story as if it were a command, so that whatever a character does becomes an example, or as if it were a bare record, so that the art of the telling is ignored. Neither does justice to what these writers made.

Hebrew narrative has a recognizable style even in translation. It moves in a chain of short clauses linked by ‘and’, because Hebrew prose uses a particular verb form (the wayyiqtol, or ‘and he did’ form) to carry the main line of events forward, one action after another. Older English versions kept many of these ‘and’s; modern ones smooth them into ‘then’, ‘so’, and ‘when’. Description is spare, speeches are short, and the pace changes sharply: years can pass in a verse, while a single conversation can take a chapter. Once a reader starts noticing these habits, the stories open up.

The modern study of the Bible as literature owes much to a handful of books from the late twentieth century. Robert Alter's The Art of Biblical Narrative (1981) showed a general readership how carefully the Hebrew stories are made. Meir Sternberg's The Poetics of Biblical Narrative (1985) worked out the theory in depth, especially the role of what the narrator leaves out. Shimon Bar-Efrat's Narrative Art in the Bible (Hebrew 1979, English 1989) and Adele Berlin's Poetics and Interpretation of Biblical Narrative (1983) are standard companions. Earlier still, the literary critic Erich Auerbach opened his book Mimesis (1946) with a famous comparison between Homer's leisurely, fully lit description in the Odyssey and the sparse, shadowed telling of Abraham's test in Genesis 22, arguing that the biblical story's silences give it a depth and a claim on the reader that Homer's surface does not. Readers who hold very different views of the Bible's history have found these studies useful, because they describe how the text works rather than how it came to be.

sections.h: The narrator: knowing everything, saying little
sections.body:
The voice that tells the Bible's stories knows things no human witness could know. It reports what God says in heaven, what characters think in private, and what happens in rooms where no one else was present. Scholars call this an omniscient narrator. Yet this all-knowing narrator is strikingly reticent. It rarely tells the reader how to feel, seldom explains motives, and almost never pauses to moralize.

The opening of Genesis 22 is a good example. The narrator tells the reader something Abraham does not know: “Some time later God tested Abraham”. Then it says almost nothing more about the inner life of anyone in the story. We are not told what Abraham felt when he heard the command, what he said to Sarah, what Isaac understood on the three-day walk, or why Abraham answered his son's question as he did. The spareness is not a lack of skill. It forces the reader to fill the silence, and the silence becomes part of the story's weight.

Because the narrator comments so rarely, the moments when it does are worth marking. After the long account of David, Bathsheba, and Uriah in 2 Samuel 11, which reports adultery, deception, and murder without a word of judgment, the chapter ends: “But the thing that David had done was evil in the sight of the LORD.” That single sentence carries more force for having been withheld. Much later, the writer of Kings summarizes David's life as faithful “except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite” (1 Kings 15:5), and the exception stands out precisely because the narrator does not otherwise hedge.

The narrator also withholds information to create suspense, irony, and surprise. Sternberg calls these withheld pieces gaps, and he distinguishes gaps the story means the reader to fill from blanks that simply do not matter. In Genesis 22 the reader knows it is a test; Abraham does not. In the book of Esther, God is never named at all, yet the reversals pile up so neatly that the reader is left to ask who arranged them, and Mordecai's question to Esther, “who knows if perhaps you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (Esther 4:14), is as close as the book comes to saying. In Ruth 2:3 the narrator says Ruth ‘happened’ to come to the field of Boaz, a phrasing that tells the reader, with a straight face, that nothing here is happening by chance.

A good first question to ask of any biblical story is therefore: what does the narrator actually say, and what does the narrator refuse to say? Many sermons and paintings supply motives and feelings the text never gives. Some of those supplements are reasonable; some change the story. Noticing the difference is the beginning of careful reading.

sections.h: Dialogue, character, and the few details that matter
sections.body:
In biblical narrative, speech does much of the work that description does in a modern novel. Alter observed that the first words a character speaks are often a key to who that character is. Esau's first recorded words, when he comes in famished and sees Jacob's stew, are those of a man ruled by his appetite (Genesis 25:30), and the narrator closes the scene by saying he despised his birthright. The serpent's first words in Genesis 3 are a question that subtly misquotes God. When a conversation is reported at length, it usually matters: the story has slowed down so the reader will listen.

Physical description is rare, and when it appears it tends to serve the plot. Esau is red and hairy because Jacob will later disguise himself with goatskins. Saul is a head taller than anyone else (1 Samuel 9:2), and the detail prepares for the moment when God tells Samuel not to consider appearance or height, because “the LORD does not see as man does” (1 Samuel 16:7). Ehud is left-handed because he will hide a dagger on his right thigh where the guards do not check (Judges 3:15-21). Readers who expect the visual richness of modern fiction can miss that almost every detail in these stories is placed for a reason.

Characters are shown more than explained, and they change. Jacob the grasping younger twin becomes, after a night of wrestling, Israel, who limps. Judah, who proposed selling Joseph, is later the brother who offers himself as a slave in place of Benjamin (Genesis 44:18-34). Saul begins modest and ends consulting a medium. David, the shepherd who trusted God against Goliath, becomes the king who stays home while his army fights (2 Samuel 11:1). The Bible's people are not flat figures of virtue or vice; they are mixed, and the stories often turn on what they become.

God is also a character in these stories, and the narrators are not shy about saying what God thinks or feels. After Saul's failure, the narrator says “the LORD regretted that He had made Saul king over Israel” (1 Samuel 15:35), in the same chapter where Samuel insists that God does not change his mind as a man does (15:29). Readers have long discussed how these belong together. Many interpreters, from the church fathers to modern theologians, read the language of divine regret as God's real personal response described in human terms, held together with his constancy; others press the tension harder. The narrative does not resolve it by argument. It sets the two sentences side by side and lets the reader hold both.

Ancient stories were heard more often than read, and biblical narrators use repetition the way a composer uses a theme. Repetition with variation is one of the most important signals in the Bible's stories. When a message is given and then delivered, or a dream is told and then retold, the reader should compare the two versions, because the differences show what a character chooses to stress, soften, or hide. Abraham's servant, retelling to Rebekah's family how he met her at the well (Genesis 24:34-49), adjusts the order of events and diplomatically reshapes his master's instructions. Pharaoh retells his dreams to Joseph with small additions of his own alarm (Genesis 41:17-24), and Joseph explains that a dream given twice means the matter is fixed (41:32).

The German Jewish thinkers Martin Buber and Franz Rosenzweig, who made a translation of the Hebrew Bible into German designed to preserve its repetitions (begun in 1925 and completed by Buber in 1961), gave the name Leitwort, ‘leading word’, to a word or root that recurs through a passage and binds it together. In the Jacob stories the words for ‘firstborn’ and ‘blessing’ (bekorah and berakah in Hebrew, which sound alike) keep returning. In the Joseph story, garments recur: the special robe, the robe dipped in blood, the garment left in the hand of Potiphar's wife, the fine linen of Pharaoh's court. Tracing such a word through a story is one of the surest ways to find its theme, and English translations that vary their vocabulary for style can hide it.

Alter borrowed from the study of Homer (where Walter Arend had described recurring scenes in 1933) the idea of the type-scene: a conventional situation that recurs in the lives of different characters, with a fixed pattern that the storyteller varies. The best-known biblical example is the meeting at a well that leads to a marriage. A man (or his agent) travels to a foreign land, meets a young woman at a well, water is drawn, the woman hurries home to tell her family, and a betrothal follows. The pattern appears with Abraham's servant and Rebekah, with Jacob and Rachel, and with Moses and the daughters of Jethro. Once a reader knows the pattern, the variations become meaningful: Rebekah draws water energetically for a whole caravan, Jacob single-handedly rolls away a stone that usually took several shepherds, and Moses drives off hostile shepherds, each detail sketching the character. Many readers see the pattern reworked in John 4, where Jesus meets a Samaritan woman at Jacob's well, with a very different outcome.

Other recurring scenes include the barren wife who is promised and then given a son (Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Samson's mother, Hannah, and in the New Testament Elizabeth), the wife passed off as a sister in a foreign court (told three times in Genesis 12, 20, and 26), and the testament of a dying leader (Jacob, Moses, Joshua, David). The pattern of the barren mother tells the reader that the child who comes is a gift and that the line of promise depends on God, not on human strength.

sections.body:
Biblical narratives are shaped at every level, from the sentence to the book. Several patterns recur often enough to watch for.

Framing and bracketing (called inclusio) mark a unit by beginning and ending it in the same way. Judges twice repeats the refrain “In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (Judges 17:6 and 21:25), bracketing the book's last and darkest stories and inviting the reader to ask whether a king will solve the problem. Samuel and Kings go on to answer: some kings help, many make it worse.

Chiasm is a mirrored arrangement, A-B-C-B-A, in which the second half retraces the first and the center is often the point of emphasis. Gordon Wenham argued in a 1978 article that the flood story in Genesis 6 to 9 is arranged as a large mirror, with the turning point at 8:1, “But God remembered Noah”. Scholars disagree about how many proposed chiasms are really in the text and how many are in the eye of the reader; the safest are those marked by repeated words rather than by general themes.

Juxtaposition places two stories side by side so that each comments on the other. Genesis 38, the story of Judah and Tamar, interrupts the Joseph story just after Joseph is sold; it shows Judah at his worst and prepares for his change in chapter 44, and it sets Judah's failure with a woman beside Joseph's integrity with Potiphar's wife in chapter 39. The book of Ruth, set “in the days when the judges ruled” (Ruth 1:1), reads as a quiet counterpoint to the violence of Judges, showing covenant faithfulness in a small town in the same dark period.

Pace is part of structure. When the narrator slows down to report a scene in detail, the moment matters; when years pass in a sentence, the story is moving to what does. Genesis spends a chapter on the purchase of a burial cave (Genesis 23) because it is Abraham's first legal foothold in the promised land. Large books are also built by headings: Genesis is organized by the repeated formula ‘these are the generations of’ (the toledot), and Kings by a regular formula that opens and closes each reign and refers the reader to royal annals for further details, as in 2 Kings 14:18.

sections.h: Why the heroes are rarely models
sections.body:
The most common mistake in reading biblical narrative is to treat every character as an example and every action as a pattern to copy. The stories themselves resist this. Abraham, the father of faith, twice passes off his wife as his sister to save himself (Genesis 12:13 and 20:2). Jacob deceives his father. Gideon, after his victory, makes a gold ephod that “became a snare to Gideon and his household” (Judges 8:27). Jephthah makes a rash vow and sacrifices his daughter. Samson breaks every part of his Nazirite vow. David commits adultery and murder, and his family life becomes a catalogue of rape, fratricide, and rebellion. Solomon, the wisest king, “did evil in the sight of the LORD” (1 Kings 11:6).

The distinction interpreters use is between description and prescription. A story describes what happened; it does not by that fact recommend it. Whether an action is approved has to be judged from the narrator's signals, from the consequences the story traces, and from the law and the prophets, which state God's will directly. Judges is especially clear on this. The book traces a downward spiral: each judge is a little more compromised than the last, until the final chapters, with no judge at all, describe a gang rape, a civil war, and the mass abduction of women, told flatly and framed by the refrain about everyone doing what was right in his own eyes. The flatness is the verdict.

This does not mean the characters teach nothing. The New Testament explicitly treats the Old Testament stories as instruction: Paul says they “were written down as warnings for us” (1 Corinthians 10:11) and that “everything that was written in the past was written for our instruction” (Romans 15:4), and Hebrews 11 holds up many of these same flawed people as examples of faith. But the faith commended is trust in God's promise, not the whole of their conduct. Hebrews names Samson, Jephthah, and Barak alongside Abraham and Moses (Hebrews 11:32), which works only if the point is what God did through people who believed him, not their moral record.

The real center of these stories is God. He keeps his promise to Abraham despite Abraham's lies, works through Jacob's scheming, and brings good out of the brothers' betrayal of Joseph, as Joseph himself says: “what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good” (Genesis 50:20). Reading the stories well means asking not first ‘how should I be like this person?’ but ‘what is God doing here, and what does it show about him?’ Christians have traditionally added a further question: how does this story belong to the larger story that runs toward Christ, the one faithful king and true son that the flawed heroes are not?

The Bible's narratives present themselves as accounts of things that happened, in real places, under named kings, often with references to sources the writer used, such as the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah. They are also shaped, selected, and told with art. Recognizing the art is not the same as denying the history; ancient historians, like modern ones, chose what to include and arranged it to make a point. Samuel-Kings and Chronicles tell much of the same history with different emphases: Chronicles, written after the exile, omits David's adultery and includes Manasseh's repentance (2 Chronicles 33:12-13), which Kings does not mention, because it is addressing a restored community concerned with the temple, the line of David, and the possibility of return to God.

How much of the history is recoverable, and how reliable the accounts are, is debated, and readers should know the main positions. Conservative scholars such as Kenneth Kitchen (On the Reliability of the Old Testament, 2003) and Iain Provan, V. Philips Long, and Tremper Longman (A Biblical History of Israel, 2003) argue that the narratives are substantially trustworthy historical sources and that archaeology, where it speaks, generally fits them. Mainstream critical scholars such as Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman (The Bible Unearthed, 2001) accept a historical core for the later monarchy but regard the patriarchal stories, the exodus, and the conquest as largely later compositions reflecting the concerns of the seventh century BC. A smaller group sometimes called minimalists, including Thomas L. Thompson, Philip R. Davies, and Niels Peter Lemche, doubted that much of the pre-exilic history can be recovered at all. Some finds have shaped this debate: the Mesha Stele (discovered in 1868) names Omri king of Israel, as 1 Kings does, and the Tel Dan inscription (found in 1993 and 1994) refers to the ‘house of David’, which weakened arguments that David was invented.

There is also a long debate about how the narrative books were composed. Jewish and Christian tradition held that Moses wrote the Pentateuch and that prophets wrote the historical books. From the eighteenth century, critical scholars proposed that the Pentateuch combines several earlier sources, a view given its classic form by Julius Wellhausen (Prolegomena to the History of Israel, 1878); since the 1970s that model has been heavily revised or abandoned by many critics (Rolf Rendtorff and R. N. Whybray among them), while conservative scholars have continued to defend substantial Mosaic origins. The book introductions in this Study Bible set out these views for each book.

Whatever position a reader takes, literary reading is common ground. A reader who thinks every detail is historically exact and a reader who doubts much of it can agree that the story of Joseph is built around garments, that Judges spirals downward, and that the narrator of Samuel withholds judgment until the last verse of 2 Samuel 11. Those observations come from the text itself.

The Gospels and Acts use many of the same techniques as the Old Testament stories, and their writers had absorbed those stories deeply, especially in their Greek translation, the Septuagint. Luke's opening chapters are full of echoes: Elizabeth is a barren wife like Sarah and Hannah, and Mary's song closely resembles Hannah's (Luke 1:46-55; 1 Samuel 2:1-10). Mark uses bracketing constantly, placing one story inside another so each interprets the other, as when the cursing of the fig tree frames the clearing of the temple (Mark 11:12-25). John uses irony in the Old Testament manner, letting characters say more than they know, as when the high priest says it is better for one man to die for the people (John 11:49-52). The separate guide on reading the Gospels treats their genre and relationships in detail.

Acts raises the question of description and prescription in a form that still divides churches. Luke tells how the first believers in Jerusalem shared their possessions (Acts 2:44-45 and 4:32), how the Spirit came in different ways and orders (Acts 2, 8, 10, and 19), and how the church chose leaders and settled disputes. Are these patterns every church should follow, or accounts of what happened at a unique moment? Pentecostal and charismatic interpreters have often read the reception of the Spirit in Acts as a normative pattern for believers after conversion; many Reformed and evangelical interpreters, such as the writers of the widely used handbook How to Read the Bible for All Its Worth (Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart, 1981; Fee himself a Pentecostal), argue that narrative sets a pattern only where the writer clearly intends it, and that what Acts reports is not automatically what Acts requires. Both sides agree that Luke is writing history with a purpose, “all that Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1) continued through his church, and that the question is how to tell what he means as example from what he means as record.

A few habits will serve a reader through every narrative in the Bible. Read the whole story, not a verse, and read it more than once; many stories run across several chapters, and the meaning of a scene often depends on where it stands. Notice where the story slows down, because that is where the narrator wants attention. Listen to the dialogue, especially first words and repeated words. Compare repeated accounts and ask what changed. Ask what the narrator says outright, which is rare and weighty, and what it leaves unsaid.

Then ask what the story shows about God, since he is the one character present in every book, and what it shows about people, since the Bible's portrait of human beings is unsparing. Ask how the story fits the larger story of the book and of the whole Bible: the promise to Abraham, the covenant at Sinai, the kingdom of David, the exile and return, and in the New Testament the coming of the one to whom Christians believe all these point.

Finally, resist the urge to turn every story into a lesson with three points. Biblical narratives often end without resolution. Genesis ends with a coffin in Egypt. Kings ends with a captive king eating at a foreign table. Jonah ends with a question God asks and the prophet never answers (Jonah 4:11). These endings are deliberate. They hand the unresolved weight to the reader, who is meant to carry the question out of the story and into life.
